claims.summary: Publish executes the source-to-target deployment. It is appropriate after authorization to apply changes, rather than for producing the requested nonexecuting approval artifact.
Script generates the proposed deployment T-SQL without applying it. Its target connection and actual deployment options determine that artifact, matching the approver's requirement.
DeployReport returns an XML summary of planned changes. It suits automated operation-level review but is not the actual executable T-SQL the approver requested.
Extract captures a live schema as a model or object files. That supports schema baselining/drift work, not this .dacpac-to-target deployment script.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: The actual deployment-review sections distinguish Script's nonexecuting T-SQL output, DeployReport's XML operations, and Extract's live-schema output. I exclude the introductory claim that every target-only object is dropped; the candidate correctly does not repeat it. The actual module/unit link and full DP-800 course/path ancestry were inspected.

The captured Deploy the project section identifies Publish as the operation that changes the target and separates Script/DeployReport preview artifacts. The stem supplies the built dacpac and authorized target access. I do not endorse the unit's blanket claim that repeated deployment changes nothing when custom scripts may execute.

choiceReviews.rationale: Publish applies changes to the target, crossing the explicit no-changes-before-approval boundary. It fits an authorized deployment, not this nonexecuting artifact-generation step.

The drift unit explicitly says Script produces the T-SQL that would execute without running it. The supplied source dacpac and target access provide the inputs for this target-specific approval artifact.
DeployReport produces an XML summary of planned operations. It is useful for automated review and is nonexecuting, but it is not the actual T-SQL required by the approver.
Extract retrieves a live schema model or object-definition files. That supports baselining and reconciliation, rather than computing the supplied dacpac's proposed target-update T-SQL.

claims.summary: Pre-deployment work occurs before schema changes and can prepare already-existing objects. It cannot insert required reference rows into a table that this initial schema deployment has not yet created.
Plain append INSERT can work for a one-time empty table. On later runs with retained stable primary keys, it does not reconcile existing rows and can raise duplicate-key errors.

A versioned post-deployment script runs after table creation and can deliberately reconcile existing and absent keys. This meets initial ordering and rerun behavior without assuming that every MERGE is concurrency-safe.

Schema-only deployment is sufficient when the application has no required seeded data or loads it separately. This workflow explicitly requires the reference rows afterward, so the model alone is incomplete.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: The actual unit places seeding after schema-plan execution, says post-deployment scripts run on every deployment, and illustrates matching existing keys and inserting absent keys. This supports ordering and repeatability, not whole-deployment atomicity or universal concurrency safety. The candidate makes neither broader claim.

choiceReviews.rationale: Pre-script timing precedes schema-plan execution. This plan first creates the lookup table, so the data-only seed has no table to populate beforehand. Pre-scripts can prepare already existing objects in other scenarios.

Appending the same stable primary keys does not reconcile existing rows. The unit warns that repeat plain INSERT seeding causes duplicate-key failures. Conditional upsert logic would be reconciliation, not this stated append-only strategy.

Post-deployment reconciliation runs after the table exists and handles both present and absent keys on later runs. These are exactly the two requirements established by the placement and idempotent-seeding sections.

The compiled declarative model supplies schema objects, not the required lookup rows. Schema-only deployment is appropriate without a seed-data requirement, but it leaves this workflow's reference data absent.

review.verificationNotes: PASS 2 only. C uniquely handles the explicit new-table first run and retained-key later runs. No particular MERGE implementation, deletion policy, concurrency guarantee or atomic transaction is assumed. Post-deployment is established GA functionality; no preview-only IDE behavior is needed. No executable seed snippet was supplied or run; review is static lifecycle/statement semantics. Intermediate fits ordering plus rerun state. The same baseline ID is a preserved refresh, not duplicate content. No construction or bounded duplicate warning occurred. d2-021 concerns project-item packaging rather than execution idempotence. The exact current subskill and real training ancestry were checked.
review.confidenceReason: High confidence in C because documented placement and repeated-key reconciliation jointly determine the answer. The strategy does not purport to validate an unseen seed implementation.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: Seed the newly modeled lookup table before the schema plan executes.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: The first deployment creates the lookup table in the schema plan, so it is not yet available at the proposed seeding time. Later-run success cannot satisfy the initial deployment requirement.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: The needed table already exists before this deployment and the data preparation must precede compatible schema changes. A script that independently creates the table would be a different, unstated workflow.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: The source distinguishes preparation before the plan from post-plan lookup population. The candidate explicitly assigns initial table creation to the plan, ruling out this timing.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: Append reference rows using INSERT after the schema deployment.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: A blind replay of the same primary keys is incorrect, but that restriction is absent from B. An append operation guarded to insert only missing keys remains an INSERT-based post-schema strategy. With unchanged reference values, that reading can satisfy the stated presence and rerun requirements.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: The required values do not change, each execution skips already present stable keys, and only missing rows are inserted after table creation. The stem does not require updating changed values, and the option does not explicitly prohibit such a guard. No particular SQL syntax or concurrency implementation is asserted.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: Write idempotent reference data scripts limits its failure warning to plain INSERT replay and demonstrates separating existing from missing keys. The authored distractor explanation adds 'without handling existing rows', which the option itself never states. This is an unexcluded contextual interpretation, not an executed counterexample.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: Use a versioned post-deployment reconciliation script for existing and missing keys.
optionChallenges.whyIncorrectInContext: Supported, not incorrect: post-plan execution gives the new table time to exist, and explicit existing/missing-key reconciliation addresses reruns. The hold concerns exclusivity against B, not C's technical soundness.
optionChallenges.couldBeCorrectWhen: The script correctly implements the reference-data policy after schema creation and handles already-present keys. Correct deletion policy, changed values and concurrent writers would need separate implementation decisions if introduced.
optionChallenges.evidenceSummary: The source describes versioning data scripts alongside schema and illustrates post-deployment matched/not-matched handling. It does not say every implementation using a different DML form is invalid.

claims.summary: A fixed sequence can be appropriate for an explicitly ordered integration journey. It does not make independent unit tests robust against leftover data or reveal their hidden state coupling.
Connectivity checks are useful smoke tests but do not verify the intended database logic. Removing value assertions hides the contamination instead of repairing test isolation.
The documented pre-test/test/post-test structure establishes inputs and cleans up to avoid contaminating subsequent tests. This addresses the state dependency while retaining meaningful assertions.
The model build does not execute test cleanup or validate deployment-script behavior. Schema validation is valuable but is not a reset of the deployed database's business data.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: The actual unit describes pre-test setup clearing leftover rows and post-test cleanup preventing contamination. It separately recommends a dedicated target and resetting known state, so production isolation does not itself isolate one test from another.

The article places pre/post scripts in the dacpac but outside object-model compilation/validation. It distinguishes build from executed data actions, not a promise that unchanged schema deployment erases business rows or that unseen cleanup is atomic.

choiceReviews.rationale: A fixed sequence can define an integration journey, but it preserves the data coupling these independent unit tests must remove. Documented reset/setup/cleanup, not a lucky order, addresses contamination.
Connection checks establish reachability, not the total-value contract. Removing the substantive assertion hides the stated defect and violates the requirement to keep meaningful expected results.

Per-test deterministic setup establishes the starting rows and cleanup removes each test's residue. This is the documented pre-test/test/post-test structure for avoiding contamination of later totals.
An object-model build does not execute database cleanup. The pre/post article separates model validation from data-script execution, so cleanup cannot be inferred from a successful build.

review.verificationNotes: PASS 2 only. C is unique given the dedicated target, residual rows and retained assertions. GA concerns established SQL Server test hooks, not a preview SDK integration. Intermediate fits the single isolation defect. The negative-wording warning protects assertion quality rather than creating ambiguity. claims.summary: The SDK's default globbing would otherwise compile the included data script as model input. Build Remove excludes it from the model while the SQLCMD include still packages it in the post-deployment script.
Removing generated outputs from source control is appropriate, but this seed file is required authored data logic. Deleting it breaks the include and loses its version history.
The product article explicitly pairs None Include with Build Remove to keep a script visible in the project view without compiling it as schema input.
The project supports one post-deployment entry point. Multiple data files are combined through SQLCMD includes; separate entry points are not the documented model for this requirement.

It treats reference-data scripts as authored versioned files, unlike generated bin/obj output. These distinct roles independently support the two selected changes.

The directly linked product article permits one pre- and one post-entry point, removes included files from model compilation, restores VS Code visibility through None, and shows the same relative-path SQLCMD syntax. Microsoft.Build.Sql combines those included files in the dacpac.

choiceReviews.rationale: Build Remove excludes the data-changing child script from default model compilation without deleting it. This is the documented handling for scripts executed through the existing SQLCMD post-deployment include.
The seed is required authored data logic, not a generated output. Removing its source-control record loses a reproducible include dependency and violates the explicit versioning requirement.
The product article adds a None item after Build Remove specifically to retain VS Code project visibility without model compilation. The existing :r continues to provide deployment inclusion.
A second independent PostDeploy entry conflicts with the documented single-entry-point model. Multiple data files must instead be invoked from the one entry point using SQLCMD includes.

Negative/pronoun warnings resolve to the named data script and entry point. Unlike direct-018 this asks about packaging, not rerun idempotence. The product article derives deploy reports and deployment T-SQL from a source model and the actual target state. This supports generating a new reviewed plan after a separate prerequisite changes that state, rather than assuming the previously calculated plan incorporates it.

The actual unit requires deployed integration tests for related operations and known state and distinguishes these from structural builds. It supports validating the complete staged sequence against the available isolated clone, not accepting a green model build as migration-safety proof.

choiceReviews.rationale: A separate controlled prerequisite stage makes its resulting schema the input for newly generated deployment planning. Reviewing that plan and testing the full sequence addresses both planning order and unvalidated script/data effects.

Pre-deployment runs before execution of an already calculated plan. The article does not provide automatic dependency replanning after the script, so retaining the rename under that assumption preserves the hazard.

Lexically renaming a file does not change its PreDeploy item semantics or the documented calculation order. It may organize files but cannot move this mutation before calculation of the existing plan.

Pre/post scripts are expressly outside object-model compilation and validation. A green build therefore cannot prove the prerequisite's target-dependent effects or the safety of the staged migration sequence.

review.verificationNotes: PASS 2 only. A uniquely changes target-state input before regenerating the plan and still validates script/data effects. The staged procedure must be derived across calculation-versus-execution and compilation-versus-deployed-behavior boundaries; unlike a setting lookup, these interdependent stages justify Advanced. Final adversarial review must still challenge depth. The isolated clone and approved window make this a test/review recommendation, not an automatic live rename, the only possible migration design, or an atomicity promise. No rename code or live SqlPackage execution was supplied; static planning semantics only. Established planning behavior is GA, independent of preview IDEs. The pronoun denotes the prerequisite. This differs from direct-017's artifact action choice, and no scoped duplicate was found.
review.confidenceReason: High confidence in A because the product ordering defeats the alternatives and the controlled staged validation follows from that ordering plus target-specific planning. No unseen migration script is attested.

optionChallenges.claimRepresented: The unchanged successful model build proves the prerequisite script and migration safe.
